originalComment: Create an Elasticsearch field name from a schema string
codeComment: The function `fix_schema` takes a `prefix` and a `schema` as input. It first extracts the schema details into a dictionary using the `extract_schema` function. Then, it converts the 'vendor' field to snake_case by replacing dots with underscores and converting to lowercase. The 'name' field is also converted to snake_case by inserting underscores before uppercase letters and converting to lowercase. The 'version' field is split by hyphens, and the first part is taken as the model. Finally, the function returns a formatted string combining the `prefix`, snake_case organization, snake_case name, and model.
codeFunctions: def fix_schema (prefix,schema):schema_dict = extract_schema (schema) snake_case_organization = schema_dict [ 'vendor' ].replace ('.','_').lower () snake_case_name = re.sub ('([^A-Z_])([A-Z])','\g<1>_\g<2>',schema_dict [ 'name' ]).lower () model = schema_dict [ 'version' ].split ('-') [ 0 ] return "{}_{}_{}_{}".format (prefix,snake_case_organization,snake_case_name,model)

### Summary:
The function `pformat_django_context_html` formats a given object into an HTML-safe string suitable for display in a Django template. It handles various types of objects, including `QuerySet`, `Manager`, strings, lazy objects, dictionaries, lists, and generic objects with a `__dict__` attribute. For `QuerySet`, it limits the output to the first 21 items and appends a truncation message if more items are present. For `Manager`, it suggests using the `.all()` method to retrieve items. Strings are escaped and formatted, lazy objects are formatted using a helper function, dictionaries and lists are formatted using specific helper functions, and objects with a `__dict__` attribute are formatted as objects. For all other types, it falls back to using `pprint` with a specified width. The output is styled using a `_style_text` function before being returned.
codeFunctions: def pformat_django_context_html (object):if isinstance (object,QuerySet):text = '' lineno = 0 for item in object.all () [:21 ]:lineno += 1 if lineno >= 21:text += u'   (remaining items truncated...)' break text += u'   {0}\n'.format (escape (repr (item))) return text elif isinstance (object,Manager):return mark_safe (u'    (use <kbd>.all</kbd> to read it)') elif isinstance (object,six.string_types):return escape (repr (object)) elif isinstance (object,Promise):# lazy() object return escape (_format_lazy (object)) elif isinstance (object,dict):# This can also be a ContextDict return _format_dict (object) elif isinstance (object,list):return _format_list (object) elif hasattr (object,'__dict__'):return _format_object (object) else:# Use regular pprint as fallback. text = DebugPrettyPrinter (width = 200).pformat (object) return _style_text (text)

### Summary:

It uses regular expressions to identify and replace patterns such as iterator objects, dynamic items, proxy objects, function methods, generators, object addresses, managers, class representations, and specific Django request fields. codeFunctions: def _style_text (text):# Escape text and apply some formatting. # To have really good highlighting, pprint would have to be re-implemented. text = escape (text) text = text.replace (' <iterator object>'," <this object can be used in a 'for' loop>") text = text.replace (' <dynamic item>',' <this object may have extra field names>') text = text.replace (' <dynamic attribute>',' <this object may have extra field names>') text = RE_PROXY.sub ('\g<1><proxy object>',text) text = RE_FUNCTION.sub ('\g<1><object method>',text) text = RE_GENERATOR.sub ("\g<1><generator, use 'for' to traverse it>",text) text = RE_OBJECT_ADDRESS.sub ('\g<1><\g<2> object>',text) text = RE_MANAGER.sub ('\g<1><manager, use .all to traverse it>',text) text = RE_CLASS_REPR.sub ('\g<1><\g<2> class>',text) # Since Django's WSGIRequest does a pprint like format for it's __repr__, make that styling consistent text = RE_REQUEST_FIELDNAME.sub ('\g<1>:\n \g<2>: ',text) text = RE_REQUEST_CLEANUP1.sub ('\g<1>',text) text = RE_REQUEST_CLEANUP2.sub (')',text) return mark_safe (text)

### Summary:
The `utf8tolatex` function converts a UTF-8 encoded string into a LaTeX-compatible string. It processes each character in the input string `s` and handles non-ASCII characters based on the provided parameters. The function normalizes the input string to NFC form and iterates through each character. If `non_ascii_only` is set to `True`, it only converts non-ASCII characters. For each character, it checks if there is a corresponding LaTeX macro in the `utf82latex` dictionary. If a macro exists, it adds it to the result, optionally enclosed in brackets. If the character is a printable ASCII character, it is added directly to the result. For non-ASCII characters without a LaTeX macro, the function logs a warning and either substitutes the character with a bold question mark (`{\bfseries ?}`) or leaves it unescaped, depending on the `substitute_bad_chars` and `fail_bad_chars` flags. If `fail_bad_chars` is `True`, it raises a `ValueError` for characters that cannot be encoded.
codeFunctions: def utf8tolatex (s,non_ascii_only = False,brackets = True,substitute_bad_chars = False,fail_bad_chars = False):s = unicode (s) # make sure s is unicode s = unicodedata.normalize ('NFC',s) if not s:return "" result = u"" for ch in s:#log.longdebug("Encoding char %r", ch) if (non_ascii_only and ord (ch) < 127):result += ch else:lch = utf82latex.get (ord (ch),None) if (lch is not None):# add brackets if needed, i.e. if we have a substituting macro. # note: in condition, beware, that lch might be of zero length. result += ('{' + lch + '}' if brackets and lch [ 0:1 ] == '\\' else lch) elif ((ord (ch) >= 32 and ord (ch) <= 127) or (ch in "\n\r\t")):# ordinary printable ascii char, just add it result += ch else:# non-ascii char msg = u"Character cannot be encoded into LaTeX: U+%04X - `%s'" % (ord (ch),ch) if fail_bad_chars:raise ValueError (msg) log.warning (msg) if substitute_bad_chars:result += r'{\bfseries ?}' else:# keep unescaped char result += ch return result

originalComment: Unpack \\ uNNNN escapes in s and encode the result as UTF - 8
codeComment:
### Summary:
The function `_unascii` processes a string `s` to handle Unicode escape sequences (`\uNNNN`). It first checks if there are any Unicode escape sequences in the string using a regular expression `_U_ESCAPE`. If no matches are found, it returns the original string or its UTF-8 encoded version depending on the Python version.

The function uses a loop to process each match found by the regular expression. It handles two cases:
1. Escaped backslashes (`\\`): These are passed through along with any preceding characters.
2. Unicode escape sequences (`\uNNNN`): These are converted to their corresponding Unicode characters. Special handling is done for surrogate pairs in Python 3 to avoid errors.

The processed parts of the string are accumulated in a list `chunks`, which are then joined and encoded to UTF-8 before returning. This method ensures efficient string manipulation and correct handling of Unicode characters across different Python versions.
codeFunctions: def _unascii (s):# make the fast path fast: if there are no matches in the string, the # whole thing is ascii. On python 2, that means we're done. On python 3, # we have to turn it into a bytes, which is quickest with encode('utf-8') m = _U_ESCAPE.search (s) if not m:return s if PY2 else s.encode ('utf-8') # appending to a string (or a bytes) is slooow, so we accumulate sections # of string result in 'chunks', and join them all together later. # (It doesn't seem to make much difference whether we accumulate # utf8-encoded bytes, or strings which we utf-8 encode after rejoining) # chunks = [ ] # 'pos' tracks the index in 's' that we have processed into 'chunks' so # far. pos = 0 while m:start = m.start () end = m.end () g = m.group (1) if g is None:# escaped backslash: pass it through along with anything before the # match chunks.append (s [ pos:end ]) else:# \uNNNN, but we have to watch out for surrogate pairs. # # On python 2, str.encode("utf-8") will decode utf-16 surrogates # before re-encoding, so it's fine for us to pass the surrogates # through. (Indeed we must, to deal with UCS-2 python builds, per # https://github.com/matrix-org/python-canonicaljson/issues/12). # # On python 3, str.encode("utf-8") complains about surrogates, so # we have to unpack them. c = int (g,16) if c < 0x20:# leave as a \uNNNN escape chunks.append (s [ pos:end ]) else:if PY3:# pragma nocover if c & 0xfc00 == 0xd800 and s [ end:end + 2 ] == '\\u':esc2 = s [ end + 2:end + 6 ] c2 = int (esc2,16) if c2 & 0xfc00 == 0xdc00:c = 0x10000 + (((c - 0xd800) << 10) | (c2 - 0xdc00)) end += 6 chunks.append (s [ pos:start ]) chunks.append (unichr (c)) pos = end m = _U_ESCAPE.search (s,pos) # pass through anything after the last match chunks.append (s [ pos:]) return (''.join (chunks)).encode ("utf-8")

### Summary:
The `singledispatchmethod` function is a decorator that allows for method overloading based on the type of the first argument after `self` (or `cls` in class methods). It uses the `singledispatch` mechanism to dispatch to the appropriate method implementation based on the type of the second argument in the function call. The `wrapper` function is created to handle the dispatching and is updated with the attributes of the original `dispatcher`. The `register` method of the `dispatcher` is exposed through the `wrapper` to allow additional type-specific implementations to be registered.
codeFunctions: def singledispatchmethod (method):dispatcher = singledispatch (method) def wrapper (* args,* * kw):return dispatcher.dispatch (args [ 1 ].__class__) (* args,* * kw) wrapper.register = dispatcher.register update_wrapper (wrapper,dispatcher) return wrapper

codeComment: The function `mark_begin_end_regex` takes a compiled regular expression (`regex`), a text string (`text`), and a list (`split_locations`) as inputs. It iterates over all matches of the regular expression in the text. For each match, it marks the positions within the match range (excluding the start position) in `split_locations` as `SHOULD_NOT_SPLIT`. It also checks the positions at the start and end of the match in `split_locations` and marks them as `SHOULD_SPLIT` if they are currently `UNDECIDED`. If the end position of the match is within the bounds of `split_locations` and is `UNDECIDED`, it is set to `SHOULD_SPLIT`. Similarly, if the start position is `UNDECIDED`, it is also set to `SHOULD_SPLIT`.
codeFunctions: def mark_begin_end_regex (regex,text,split_locations):for match in regex.finditer (text):end_match = match.end () begin_match = match.start () for i in range (begin_match + 1,end_match):split_locations [ i ] = SHOULD_NOT_SPLIT if end_match < len (split_locations):if split_locations [ end_match ] == UNDECIDED:split_locations [ end_match ] = SHOULD_SPLIT if split_locations [ begin_match ] == UNDECIDED:split_locations [ begin_match ] = SHOULD_SPLIT

The higher 8 bits of the integer are stored in the first byte, and the lower 8 bits are stored in the second byte. The function then returns this 2-byte bytearray.
codeFunctions: def encode16Int (value):value = int (value) encoded = bytearray (2) encoded [ 0 ] = value >> 8 encoded [ 1 ] = value & 0xFF return encoded

originalComment: Encodes value into a multibyte sequence defined by MQTT protocol.Used to encode packet length fields.
codeComment: The `encodeLength` function encodes a given integer value into a bytearray using a variable-length encoding scheme. The function repeatedly extracts the least significant 7 bits of the value, sets the 8th bit if there are more bits to encode, and appends the result to a bytearray. This process continues until the entire value is encoded. The function then returns the encoded bytearray.
codeFunctions: def encodeLength (value):encoded = bytearray () while True:digit = value % 128 value //= 128 if value > 0:digit |= 128 encoded.append (digit) if value <= 0:break return encoded

originalComment: Decodes a variable length value defined in the MQTT protocol.This value typically represents remaining field lengths
codeComment: The function `decodeLength` decodes a length value that has been encoded using a variable-length format, often seen in protocols like Protocol Buffers. It processes each byte of the input `encoded` list, extracting the lower 7 bits of each byte and using them to build the final length value. The `multiplier` variable keeps track of the position of the current byte in the encoded length, multiplying by 128 (0x80) for each subsequent byte. The loop continues until a byte is encountered that does not have its 8th bit set (i.e., the byte does not have the value 0x80 when bitwise ANDed with 0x80), indicating the end of the encoded length. The function then returns the fully decoded length value.
codeFunctions: def decodeLength (encoded):value = 0 multiplier = 1 for i in encoded:value += (i & 0x7F) * multiplier multiplier *= 0x80 if (i & 0x80) != 0x80:break return value

originalComment: Encode and store a CONNECT control packet.
codeComment:
### Summary:
The `encode` method constructs a MQTT CONNECT packet by encoding various components into a byte array. It starts by initializing the header, variable header, and payload byte arrays. The header is set with a packet code of `0x10`. The variable header includes the encoded version tag, protocol level, and flags that indicate options like clean start, will message, username, and password. The keepalive value is also added to the variable header. The payload section includes the client ID and, if applicable, the will topic, will message, username, and password. Finally, the method calculates the total length of the variable header and payload, encodes this length, and appends it to the header. The complete packet is then built by extending the header with the variable header and payload. The method returns the encoded packet as a string in Python 2 or bytes in Python 3.
codeFunctions: def encode (self):header = bytearray (1) varHeader = bytearray () payload = bytearray () header [ 0 ] = 0x10 # packet code # ---- Variable header encoding section ----- varHeader.extend (encodeString (self.version [ 'tag' ])) varHeader.append (self.version [ 'level' ]) # protocol Level flags = (self.cleanStart << 1) if self.willTopic is not None and self.willMessage is not None:flags |= 0x04 | (self.willRetain << 5) | (self.willQoS << 3) if self.username is not None:flags |= 0x80 if self.password is not None:flags |= 0x40 varHeader.append (flags) varHeader.extend (encode16Int (self.keepalive)) # ------ Payload encoding section ---- payload.extend (encodeString (self.clientId)) if self.willTopic is not None and self.willMessage is not None:payload.extend (encodeString (self.willTopic)) payload.extend (encodeString (self.willMessage)) if self.username is not None:payload.extend (encodeString (self.username)) if self.password is not None:payload.extend (encode16Int (len (self.password))) payload.extend (bytearray (self.password,encoding = 'ascii',errors = 'ignore')) # ---- Build the packet once all lengths are known ---- header.extend (encodeLength (len (varHeader) + len (payload))) header.extend (varHeader) header.extend (payload) self.encoded = header return str (header) if PY2 else bytes (header)

originalComment: Decode a CONNECT control packet.
codeComment:
### Summary:
The `decode` method processes a given MQTT packet to extract and set various properties based on the MQTT protocol specifications. Here's a breakdown of the method:

1. **Initialization**: The method starts by storing the input `packet` in `self.encoded`.

2. **Determine Length of Length Field**: It calculates the length of the variable length field by checking the continuation bit (0x80) in each byte of the length field.

3. **Extract Remaining Packet**: After determining the length of the length field, it extracts the remaining part of the packet.

4. **Decode Variable Header**:
   - **Version String**: Decodes the version string from the remaining packet.
   - **Version ID**: Converts the version string to an integer and sets `self.version` to either `v31` or `v311` based on the version ID.
   - **Flags**: Extracts various flags from the next byte of the packet:
     - `cleanStart`: Indicates whether the session should be started fresh.
     - `willFlag`: Indicates whether a Will Message is included.
     - `willQoS`: Quality of Service level for the Will Message.
     - `willRetain`: Indicates whether the Will Message should be retained.
     - `userFlag`: Indicates whether a username is included.
     - `passFlag`: Indicates whether a password is included.
   - **Keep Alive**: Decodes the keep alive period from the next two bytes of the packet.

5. **Decode Payload**:
   - **Client ID**: Decodes the client ID from the remaining packet.
   - **Will Message Details**: If `willFlag` is set, it decodes the Will Topic and Will Message.
   - **Username**: If `userFlag` is set, it decodes the username.
   - **Password**: If `passFlag` is set, it decodes the password.

This method effectively parses an MQTT CONNECT packet, extracting all necessary information to establish a connection with an MQTT broker.
codeFunctions: def decode (self,packet):self.encoded = packet # Strip the fixed header plus variable length field lenLen = 1 while packet [ lenLen ] & 0x80:lenLen += 1 packet_remaining = packet [ lenLen + 1:] # Variable Header version_str,packet_remaining = decodeString (packet_remaining) version_id = int (packet_remaining [ 0 ]) if version_id == v31 [ 'level' ]:self.version = v31 else:self.version = v311 flags = packet_remaining [ 1 ] self.cleanStart = (flags & 0x02) != 0 willFlag = (flags & 0x04) != 0 willQoS = (flags >> 3) & 0x03 willRetain = (flags & 0x20) != 0 userFlag = (flags & 0x80) != 0 passFlag = (flags & 0x40) != 0 packet_remaining = packet_remaining [ 2:] self.keepalive = decode16Int (packet_remaining) # Payload packet_remaining = packet_remaining [ 2:] self.clientId,packet_remaining = decodeString (packet_remaining) if willFlag:self.willRetain = willRetain self.willQoS = willQoS self.willTopic,packet_remaining = decodeString (packet_remaining) self.willMessage,packet_remaining = decodeString (packet_remaining) if userFlag:self.username,packet_remaining = decodeString (packet_remaining) if passFlag:l = decode16Int (packet_remaining) self.password = packet_remaining [ 2:2 + l ]

codeComment:
### Summary:
The `decode` method processes a packet to extract and store specific information. It first assigns the entire packet to `self.encoded`. Then, it calculates the length of the variable length field by iterating through bytes until it finds a byte not having the 8th bit set (0x80). After determining the length of the variable length field, it extracts the remaining part of the packet. From this remaining part, it sets `self.session` to `True` if the least significant bit of the first byte is 1, otherwise `False`. It also extracts the second byte and converts it to an integer, storing it in `self.resultCode`.
codeFunctions: def decode (self,packet):self.encoded = packet # Strip the fixed header plus variable length field lenLen = 1 while packet [ lenLen ] & 0x80:lenLen += 1 packet_remaining = packet [ lenLen + 1:] self.session = (packet_remaining [ 0 ] & 0x01) == 0x01 self.resultCode = int (packet_remaining [ 1 ])

### Summary:

Depending on the Quality of Service (QoS) level, it sets the appropriate flags in the `header`. The topic name is encoded and added to `varHeader`. The payload is then processed: if it's a `bytearray`, it's directly added; if it's a string, it's converted to a `bytearray` using UTF-8 encoding. If the payload type is neither `bytearray` nor `str`, a `PayloadTypeError` is raised. The total length of `varHeader` and `payload` is calculated, and if it exceeds 268,435,455, a `PayloadValueError` is raised. The length is then encoded and added to `header`, followed by `varHeader` and `payload`. Finally, the complete encoded message is stored in `self.encoded` and returned as a string in Python 2 or bytes in Python 3.
codeFunctions: def encode (self):header = bytearray (1) varHeader = bytearray () payload = bytearray () if self.qos:header [ 0 ] = 0x30 | self.retain | (self.qos << 1) | (self.dup << 3) varHeader.extend (encodeString (self.topic)) # topic name varHeader.extend (encode16Int (self.msgId)) # msgId should not be None else:header [ 0 ] = 0x30 | self.retain varHeader.extend (encodeString (self.topic)) # topic name if isinstance (self.payload,bytearray):payload.extend (self.payload) elif isinstance (self.payload,str):payload.extend (bytearray (self.payload,encoding = 'utf-8')) else:raise PayloadTypeError (type (self.payload)) totalLen = len (varHeader) + len (payload) if totalLen > 268435455:raise PayloadValueError (totalLen) header.extend (encodeLength (totalLen)) header.extend (varHeader) header.extend (payload) self.encoded = header return str (header) if PY2 else bytes (header)

originalComment: Decode a PUBLISH control packet.
codeComment:
### Summary:
The `decode` method processes an MQTT packet to extract various components such as the topic, message ID, and payload. It starts by determining the length of the length field (`lenLen`) which is variable. It then parses the first byte to extract flags indicating whether the message is a duplicate (`dup`), its Quality of Service level (`qos`), and whether it should be retained (`retain`). The method decodes the topic from the remaining packet. If the QoS level is greater than 0, it also extracts a message ID. Finally, it extracts the payload from the packet.
codeFunctions: def decode (self,packet):self.encoded = packet lenLen = 1 while packet [ lenLen ] & 0x80:lenLen += 1 packet_remaining = packet [ lenLen + 1:] self.dup = (packet [ 0 ] & 0x08) == 0x08 self.qos = (packet [ 0 ] & 0x06) >> 1 self.retain = (packet [ 0 ] & 0x01) == 0x01 self.topic,_ = decodeString (packet_remaining) topicLen = decode16Int (packet_remaining) if self.qos:self.msgId = decode16Int (packet_remaining [ topicLen + 2:topicLen + 4 ]) self.payload = packet_remaining [ topicLen + 4:] else:self.msgId = None self.payload = packet_remaining [ topicLen + 2:]

The `fastsmooth` function applies a moving average smoothing to an input array `a` using a specified window size `win`. If the window size is even, it increments the window size by 1 to ensure it is odd. The function creates a kernel of ones divided by the window size to compute the average. It then pads the start and end of the array with the mean of the initial and final segments of the array, respectively, to maintain the array length after convolution. The function returns the smoothed array by concatenating the padded start, the convolution of the array with the kernel, and the padded end.
codeFunctions: def fastsmooth (a,win = 11):# check to see if 'window' is odd (even does not work) if win % 2 == 0:win += 1 # add 1 to window if it is even. kernel = np.ones (win) / win npad = int ((win - 1) / 2) spad = np.full (npad + 1,np.mean (a [:(npad + 1) ])) epad = np.full (npad - 1,np.mean (a [ - (npad - 1):])) return np.concatenate ([ spad,np.convolve (a,kernel,'valid'),epad ])

originalComment: Identify clusters using DBSCAN algorithm.
codeComment:
### Summary:
The `cluster_DBSCAN` function performs clustering on the input data using the DBSCAN algorithm. It accepts parameters such as `data`, `eps`, `min_samples`, `n_clusters`, and `maxiter`. If `n_clusters` is not specified, it uses the provided `eps` and `min_samples` to fit the DBSCAN model. If `n_clusters` is specified, the function iteratively adjusts the `eps` value to find the desired number of clusters, starting from an initial `eps` of 1/0.95 and decreasing it by multiplying with 0.95 in each iteration. The process stops when the number of clusters matches `n_clusters` or when the maximum number of iterations (`maxiter`) is reached. The function returns the cluster labels and a mask indicating core samples. If the desired number of clusters is not found within the maximum iterations, a warning is issued.

def cluster_DBSCAN (data,eps = None,min_samples = None,n_clusters = None,maxiter = 200,* * kwargs):if n_clusters is None:if eps is None:eps = 0.3 db = cl.DBSCAN (eps = eps,min_samples = min_samples,* * kwargs).fit (data) else:clusters = 0 eps_temp = 1 / .95 niter = 0 while clusters < n_clusters:clusters_last = clusters eps_temp *= 0.95 db = cl.DBSCAN (eps = eps_temp,min_samples = min_samples,* * kwargs).fit (data) clusters = (len (set (db.labels_)) - (1 if - 1 in db.labels_ else 0)) if clusters < clusters_last:eps_temp *= 1 / 0.95 db = cl.DBSCAN (eps = eps_temp,min_samples = min_samples,* * kwargs).fit (data) clusters = (len (set (db.labels_)) - (1 if - 1 in db.labels_ else 0)) warnings.warn (('

***Unable to find {:.0f} clusters in ' 'data. Found {:.0f} with an eps of {:.2e}' '').format (n_clusters,clusters,eps_temp)) break niter += 1 if niter == maxiter:warnings.warn (('

***Maximum iterations ({:.0f}) reached' ', {:.0f} clusters not found.
Deacrease ' 'min_samples or n_clusters (or increase ' 'maxiter).').format (maxiter,n_clusters)) break labels = db.labels_ core_samples_mask = np.zeros_like (labels) core_samples_mask [ db.core_sample_indices_ ] = True return labels,core_samples_mask

codeComment:
### Summary:
The `exclude_downhole` function takes a boolean array `filt` and an optional `threshold` parameter (default is 2). It creates a copy of `filt` named `cfilt`. The function identifies the indices of `False` values in `filt` using `bool_2_indices`. It then checks if the differences between these indices are greater than or equal to the `threshold`. If such differences exist, it sets all values in `cfilt` to `False` starting from the second index where the difference condition is met. Finally, it returns the modified `cfilt` array.
codeFunctions: def exclude_downhole (filt,threshold = 2):cfilt = filt.copy () inds = bool_2_indices (~ filt) rem = (np.diff (inds) >= threshold) [:,0 ] if any (rem):if inds [ rem ].shape [ 0 ] > 1:limit = inds [ rem ] [ 1,0 ] cfilt [ limit:] = False return cfilt

### Summary:
The `defrag` function processes a boolean array `filt` to either include or exclude contiguous segments based on a specified `threshold` and `mode`. It uses a helper function `bool_2_indices` to convert boolean indices to their respective positions. If `mode` is 'include', it identifies segments to include; if 'exclude', it identifies segments to exclude. Segments shorter than or equal to the `threshold` are either set to `True` (include) or `False` (exclude) in the output array `cfilt`. If no segments meet the criteria, the original `filt` is returned unchanged.
codeFunctions: def defrag (filt,threshold = 3,mode = 'include'):if bool_2_indices (filt) is None:return filt if mode == 'include':inds = bool_2_indices (~ filt) + 1 rep = True if mode == 'exclude':inds = bool_2_indices (filt) + 1 rep = False rem = (np.diff (inds) <= threshold) [:,0 ] cfilt = filt.copy () if any (rem):for lo,hi in inds [ rem ]:cfilt [ lo:hi ] = rep return cfilt

codeFunctions: def despike (self,expdecay_despiker = True,exponent = None,noise_despiker = True,win = 3,nlim = 12.,maxiter = 3):if not hasattr (self,'despiked'):self.data [ 'despiked' ] = Bunch () out = { } for a,v in self.focus.items ():if 'time' not in a.lower ():sig = v.copy () # copy data if expdecay_despiker:if exponent is not None:sig = proc.expdecay_despike (sig,exponent,self.tstep,maxiter) else:warnings.warn ('exponent is None - either provide exponent, or run at `analyse`\nlevel to automatically calculate it.') if noise_despiker:sig = proc.noise_despike (sig,int (win),nlim,maxiter) out [ a ] = sig self.data [ 'despiked' ].update (out) # recalculate total counts self.data [ 'total_counts' ] = sum (self.data [ 'despiked' ].values ()) self.setfocus ('despiked') return

originalComment: Transform boolean arrays into list of limit pairs.
codeComment:
### Summary:
The `mkrngs` method processes boolean arrays (`self.bkg`, `self.sig`, `self.trn`) to extract corresponding time ranges from `self.Time`. It uses a helper function `bool_2_indices` to convert boolean arrays to index arrays. If the boolean array is not `None`, it slices `self.Time` using these indices to create background (`self.bkgrng`), signal (`self.sigrng`), and training (`self.trnrng`) time ranges. If any boolean array is `None`, it assigns a default range of `[np.nan, np.nan]` to the respective time range.

Additionally, the method initializes an array `self.ns` to label contiguous segments of `True` values in `self.sig`. Each segment is assigned a unique number, and `self.n` is set to the maximum number of these segments, effectively counting the number of traces.
codeFunctions: def mkrngs (self):bbool = bool_2_indices (self.bkg) if bbool is not None:self.bkgrng = self.Time [ bbool ] else:self.bkgrng = [ [ np.nan,np.nan ] ] sbool = bool_2_indices (self.sig) if sbool is not None:self.sigrng = self.Time [ sbool ] else:self.sigrng = [ [ np.nan,np.nan ] ] tbool = bool_2_indices (self.trn) if tbool is not None:self.trnrng = self.Time [ tbool ] else:self.trnrng = [ [ np.nan,np.nan ] ] self.ns = np.zeros (self.Time.size) n = 1 for i in range (len (self.sig) - 1):if self.sig [ i ]:self.ns [ i ] = n if self.sig [ i ] and ~ self.sig [ i + 1 ]:n += 1 self.n = int (max (self.ns)) # record number of traces return

codeFunctions: def ratio (self,internal_standard = None):if internal_standard is not None:self.internal_standard = internal_standard self.data [ 'ratios' ] = Bunch () for a in self.analytes:self.data [ 'ratios' ] [ a ] = (self.data [ 'bkgsub' ] [ a ] / self.data [ 'bkgsub' ] [ self.internal_standard ]) self.setfocus ('ratios') return

### Summary:
The `calibrate` method calibrates the data for specified analytes using provided calibration parameters. If no analytes are specified, it defaults to using all analytes stored in `self.analytes`. The method checks if the 'calibrated' key exists in `self.data`; if not, it initializes it as a `Bunch` object. For each analyte, it retrieves the slope (`m`) and intercept (`c`) from `calib_ps`, applies these to the corresponding ratios in `self.data['ratios']`, and stores the results in `self.data['calibrated']`. If the internal standard is not among the specified analytes, it initializes an empty array for it in `self.data['calibrated']`. Finally, it sets the focus to 'calibrated' and returns.
codeFunctions: def calibrate (self,calib_ps,analytes = None):# can have calibration function stored in self and pass *coefs? if analytes is None:analytes = self.analytes if 'calibrated' not in self.data.keys ():self.data [ 'calibrated' ] = Bunch () for a in analytes:m = calib_ps [ a ] [ 'm' ].new (self.uTime) if 'c' in calib_ps [ a ]:c = calib_ps [ a ] [ 'c' ].new (self.uTime) else:c = 0 self.data [ 'calibrated' ] [ a ] = self.data [ 'ratios' ] [ a ] * m + c if self.internal_standard not in analytes:self.data [ 'calibrated' ] [ self.internal_standard ] = np.empty (len (self.data [ 'ratios' ] [ self.internal_standard ])) self.setfocus ('calibrated') return

originalComment: Function for calculating the ablation time for each ablation.

### Summary:
The `ablation_times` method calculates the duration of ablation events for different numbers of ablations. It initializes an empty dictionary `ats` to store the results. For each number `n` from 1 to `self.n`, it extracts the times corresponding to `n` ablations from `self.Time` where `self.ns` equals `n`. It then calculates the difference between the maximum and minimum times for these events and stores this duration in `ats` with the key `n-1`. codeFunctions: def ablation_times (self):ats = { } for n in np.arange (self.n) + 1:t = self.Time [ self.ns == n ] ats [ n - 1 ] = t.max () - t.min () return ats

originalComment: Calculate local correlation between two analytes.
codeComment:
### Summary:
The `calc_correlation` method calculates the Pearson correlation coefficient between two analytes (`x_analyte` and `y_analyte`) over a specified rolling window. The method accepts parameters for the window size, whether to apply a filter, and whether to recalculate the correlation if it has already been computed. It ensures the window size is odd, applies a filter if specified, and computes the rolling correlation using the Pearson correlation coefficient, handling NaN values appropriately. The results are stored and returned.
codeFunctions: def calc_correlation (self,x_analyte,y_analyte,window = 15,filt = True,recalc = True):label = '{:}_{:}_{:.0f}'.format (x_analyte,y_analyte,window) if label in self.correlations and not recalc:return # make window odd if window % 2 != 1:window += 1 # get filter ind = self.filt.grab_filt (filt,[ x_analyte,y_analyte ]) x = nominal_values (self.focus [ x_analyte ]) x [ ~ ind ] = np.nan xr = rolling_window (x,window,pad = np.nan) y = nominal_values (self.focus [ y_analyte ]) y [ ~ ind ] = np.nan yr = rolling_window (y,window,pad = np.nan) r,p = zip (* map (nan_pearsonr,xr,yr)) r = np.array (r) p = np.array (p) # save correlation info self.correlations [ label ] = r,p return

originalComment: Calculate correlation filter.
codeComment:
### Summary:
The `filter_correlation` method calculates and filters the correlation between two analytes (`x_analyte` and `y_analyte`) based on specified parameters. It ensures the window size is odd, computes the correlation, and applies a filter based on correlation (`r`) and p-value (`p`) thresholds. The method then adds this filter to the filter set, turns it off, and turns it on for the `y_analyte`. The filter is named using the analyte names and window size.
codeFunctions: def filter_correlation (self,x_analyte,y_analyte,window = 15,r_threshold = 0.9,p_threshold = 0.05,filt = True,recalc = False):# make window odd if window % 2 != 1:window += 1 params = locals () del (params [ 'self' ]) setn = self.filt.maxset + 1 label = '{:}_{:}_{:.0f}'.format (x_analyte,y_analyte,window) self.calc_correlation (x_analyte,y_analyte,window,filt,recalc) r,p = self.correlations [ label ] cfilt = (abs (r) > r_threshold) & (p < p_threshold) cfilt = ~ cfilt name = x_analyte + '_' + y_analyte + '_corr' self.filt.add (name = name,filt = cfilt,info = (x_analyte + ' vs. ' + y_analyte + ' correlation filter.'),params = params,setn = setn) self.filt.off (filt = name) self.filt.on (analyte = y_analyte,filt = name) return

### Summary:
The `summary_stats` function calculates and returns a DataFrame containing summary statistics and test results for two input arrays `x` and `y`. The function performs the following steps:

1. **Initialization**: 
   - Creates a DataFrame `out` with a MultiIndex for columns to store various statistics and test results.
   - If `nm` is a string, it converts it into a list.

2. **Data Cleaning**:
   - Removes any rows where either `x` or `y` is NaN.

3. **Residual Calculation**:
   - Computes the residuals `r` as the difference between `y` and `x`.

4. **Summary Statistics**:
   - Calculates and stores the number of observations (`N`), median, lower quartile (`LQ`), interquartile range (`IQR`), and upper quartile (`UQ`) of the residuals.

5. **Kolmogorov-Smirnov Test**:
   - Performs a two-sample Kolmogorov-Smirnov test to compare the distributions of `x` and `y` and stores the test statistic and p-value.

6. **Residual Regression Analysis**:
   - Fits an ordinary least squares (OLS) regression model to the residuals with `x` as the predictor.
   - Stores the intercept, slope, their respective t-values, p-values, and the adjusted R-squared value of the regression model.

7. **Return**:
   - Returns the DataFrame `out` containing all the calculated statistics and test results.

x # summary statistics cat = 'Residual Summary' out.loc [:,(cat,'N') ] = len (x) out.loc [:,(cat,'Median') ] = np.median (r) out.loc [:,[ (cat,'LQ'),(cat,'UQ') ] ] = np.percentile (r,[ 25,75 ]) out.loc [:,(cat,'IQR') ] = out.loc [:,(cat,'UQ') ] - out.loc [:,(cat,'LQ') ] # non-paired test for same distribution cat = 'Kolmogorov-Smirnov' ks = stats.ks_2samp (x,y) out.loc [:,(cat,'KS') ] = ks.statistic out.loc [:,(cat,'p') ] = ks.pvalue # regression analysis of residuals - slope should be 0, intercept should be 0 cat = 'Residual Regression' X = sm.add_constant (x) reg = sm.OLS (r,X,missing = 'drop') fit = reg.fit () out.loc [:,[ (cat,'Intercept'),(cat,'Slope') ] ] = fit.params out.loc [:,[ (cat,'Intercept t'),(cat,'Slope t') ] ] = fit.tvalues out.loc [:,(cat,'R2') ] = fit.rsquared out.loc [:,[ (cat,'Intercept p'),(cat,'Slope p') ] ] = fit.pvalues return out

### Summary:
The `lookup` method is designed to find a `TypeClass` associated with a given type `G` in the context of another type `TC`. It first checks if `G` is a string and raises an `ImplicitNotFound` exception if true. It then verifies if `G` is an instance of `type`, `TypeVar`, or `_GenericAlias`; otherwise, it raises an `ImplicitNotFound` exception.

The method defines a `match` function that uses `_lookup_type` to find a `TypeClass` for a given type. It also defines an `attach_type` function to set the `tpe` attribute of a `TypeClass` to `G`.

The method determines the `scrutinee` based on whether `G` is a `TypeVar` and whether it has a bound. It then determines the `target` type, which is either the origin of `scrutinee` if `scrutinee` is a `_GenericAlias` or `scrutinee` itself. The method retrieves the method resolution order (MRO) of the `target` type.

Finally, the method iterates over the MRO, applies the `match` function to each type, and returns the first `TypeClass` found, with the `tpe` attribute attached. If no `TypeClass` is found, it returns `None`.
codeFunctions: def lookup (self,TC:type,G:type) -> Optional [ TypeClass ]:if isinstance (G,str):raise ImplicitNotFound (TC,G,f'{G} is a string annotation') if not isinstance (G,(type,TypeVar,_GenericAlias)):raise ImplicitNotFound (TC,G,f'{G} is neither type, _GenericAlias nor TypeVar: {type(G)}') match = lambda a:self._lookup_type (TC,a) def attach_type (tc:TypeClass) -> TypeClass:setattr (tc,'tpe',G) return tc scrutinee = ((unbounded_typevar (TC,G) if G.__bound__ is None else G.__bound__) if isinstance (G,TypeVar) else G) safe_mro = lambda t:getattr (t,'__mro__',(t,)) target = scrutinee.__origin__ if isinstance (scrutinee,_GenericAlias) else scrutinee mro = safe_mro (target) return next ((attach_type (a) for a in map (match,mro) if a is not None),None)

### Summary:
The function `calc_M` calculates the molecular mass of a given molecule based on its chemical formula. It uses a periodic table to look up atomic weights and percentages. The function handles both subgroups enclosed in parentheses and the main part of the molecular formula. It uses regular expressions to parse the formula, identify elements and their counts, and compute the total molecular mass by summing the contributions of each element, taking into account any subgroups and their multipliers.
codeFunctions: def calc_M (molecule):# load periodic table els = elements () # define regexs parens = re.compile ('\(([A-z0-9]+)\)([0-9]+)?') stoich = re.compile ('([A-Z][a-z]?)([0-9]+)?') ps = parens.findall (molecule) # find subgroups in parentheses rem = parens.sub ('',molecule) # get remainder m = 0 # deal with sub-groups if len (ps) > 0:for sub,ns in ps:ms = 0 for e,n in stoich.findall (sub):me = (els.loc [ e,'atomic_weight' ] * els.loc [ e,'percent' ] / 100).sum () if n == '':n = 1 else:n = int (n) ms += me * n if ns == '':ns = 1 else:ns = int (ns) m += ms * ns # deal with remainder for e,n in stoich.findall (rem):me = (els.loc [ e,'atomic_weight' ] * els.loc [ e,'percent' ] / 100).sum () if n == '':n = 1 else:n = int (n) m += me * n return m

### Summary:
The `annihilate` function takes two tuples as input: `predicate` and `stack`. It filters out elements from `stack` that are present in `predicate` and stores the result in `extra`. codeFunctions: def annihilate (predicate:tuple,stack:tuple) -> tuple:extra = tuple (filter (lambda x:x not in predicate,stack)) head = reduce (lambda x,y:y if y in predicate else x,stack,None) return extra + (head,) if head else extra

originalComment: Calculate gaussian weigted moving mean SD and SE.
codeComment:
### Summary:
The `gauss_weighted_stats` function calculates weighted statistics (mean, standard deviation, and standard error) for a set of data points using Gaussian weighting. The function takes four parameters: `x` (the x-coordinates of the data points), `yarray` (the y-values corresponding to each x-coordinate), `x_new` (the new x-coordinates at which to calculate the statistics), and `fwhm` (the full width at half maximum of the Gaussian kernel).

1. **Gaussian Kernel Calculation**: The standard deviation (`sigma`) of the Gaussian kernel is calculated from the `fwhm`.
2. **Mask Creation**: A mask array is created to store the Gaussian weights for each combination of `x`, `yarray`, and `x_new`.
3. **Mask Filling**: The mask is filled with Gaussian weights for each `x_new` value.
4. **Normalization**: The mask is normalized so that the sum of the Gaussian weights for each `x_new` is 1.
5. **Weighted Mean Calculation**: The weighted mean (`av`) is calculated by applying the normalized mask to the `yarray` and summing along the `x` axis.
6. **Weighted Standard Deviation Calculation**: The weighted standard deviation (`std`) is calculated by first determining the squared differences between the weighted mean and the `yarray` values, applying the mask, and then taking the square root of the weighted average of these squared differences.
7. **Standard Error Calculation**: The standard error (`se`) is calculated by dividing the standard deviation by the square root of the sum of the weights for each `x_new`.

The function returns the weighted mean, weighted standard deviation, and standard error for the data points at the specified `x_new` coordinates.
codeFunctions: def gauss_weighted_stats (x,yarray,x_new,fwhm):sigma = fwhm / (2 * np.sqrt (2 * np.log (2))) # create empty mask array mask = np.zeros ((x.size,yarray.shape [ 1 ],x_new.size)) # fill mask for i,xni in enumerate (x_new):mask [:,:,i ] = gauss (x [:,np.newaxis ],1,xni,sigma) # normalise mask nmask = mask / mask.sum (0) # sum of each gaussian = 1 # calculate moving average av = (nmask * yarray [:,:,np.newaxis ]).sum (0) # apply mask to data # sum along xn axis to get means # calculate moving sd diff = np.power (av - yarray [:,:,np.newaxis ],2) std = np.sqrt ((diff * nmask).sum (0)) # sqrt of weighted average of data-mean # calculate moving se se = std / np.sqrt (mask.sum (0)) # max amplitude of weights is 1, so sum of weights scales # a fn of how many points are nearby. Use this as 'n' in # SE calculation. return av,std,se

originalComment: Gaussian function.
codeComment:
### Summary:
The function `gauss` calculates the value of a Gaussian (normal) distribution at a given point `x` using the parameters `A`, `mu`, and `sigma`. Here, `A` is the amplitude, `mu` is the mean, and `sigma` is the standard deviation of the distribution. The function returns the computed Gaussian value using the formula:

\[ \text{Gaussian}(x) = A \times \exp\left(-\frac{0.5 \times (x - \mu)^2}{\sigma^2}\right) \]
codeFunctions: def gauss (x,* p):A,mu,sigma = p return A * np.exp (- 0.5 * (- mu + x) ** 2 / sigma ** 2)

originalComment: Calculate a gradient threshold filter to the data.
codeComment:
### Summary:
The `filter_gradient_threshold_percentile` method filters samples based on the gradient of a specified analyte, using percentile thresholds. It calculates the gradients of the analyte for all samples within a given window size and applies a filter based on the specified percentiles. The method supports both population-level and individual-level filtering. For population-level filtering, it calculates the percentile limits across all samples and applies these limits to each sample. For individual-level filtering, it calculates the percentile limits for each sample individually. The method adds filter results to the sample's filter set, indicating which gradients are above, below, or within the specified percentile thresholds.
codeFunctions: def filter_gradient_threshold_percentile (self,analyte,percentiles,level = 'population',win = 15,filt = False,samples = None,subset = None):params = locals () del (params [ 'self' ]) if samples is not None:subset = self.make_subset (samples) samples = self._get_samples (subset) self.minimal_analytes.update ([ analyte ]) # Calculate gradients of all samples self.get_gradients (analytes = [ analyte ],win = win,filt = filt,subset = subset) grad = self.gradients [ analyte ] [ ~ np.isnan (self.gradients [ analyte ]) ] if isinstance (percentiles,(int,float)):percentiles = [ percentiles ] if level == 'population':# calculate filter limits lims = np.percentile (grad,percentiles) # Calculate filter for individual samples with self.pbar.set (total = len (samples),desc = 'Percentile Threshold Filter') as prog:for s in samples:d = self.data [ s ] setn = d.filt.maxset + 1 g = calc_grads (d.Time,d.focus,[ analyte ],win) [ analyte ] if level == 'individual':gt = nominal_values (g) lims = np.percentile (gt [ ~ np.isnan (gt) ],percentiles) if len (lims) == 1:above = g >= lims [ 0 ] below = g < lims [ 0 ] d.filt.add (analyte + '_{:.1f}-grd-pcnt_below'.format (percentiles [ 0 ]),below,'Gradients below {:.1f}th {:} percentile ({:.2e})'.format (percentiles [ 0 ],analyte,lims [ 0 ]),params,setn = setn) d.filt.add (analyte + '_{:.1f}-grd-pcnt_above'.format (percentiles [ 0 ]),above,'Gradients above {:.1f}th {:} percentile ({:.2e})'.format (percentiles [ 0 ],analyte,lims [ 0 ]),params,setn = setn) elif len (lims) == 2:inside = (g >= min (lims)) & (g <= max (lims)) outside = (g < min (lims)) | (g > max (lims)) lpc = '-'.join ([ '{:.1f}'.format (p) for p in percentiles ]) d.filt.add (analyte + '_' + lpc + '-grd-pcnt_inside',inside,'Gradients between ' + lpc + ' ' + analyte + 'percentiles',params,setn = setn) d.filt.add (analyte + '_' + lpc + '-grd-pcnt_outside',outside,'Gradients outside ' + lpc + ' ' + analyte + 'percentiles',params,setn = setn) prog.update () return

codeFunctions: def by_regex (file,outdir = None,split_pattern = None,global_header_rows = 0,fname_pattern = None,trim_tail_lines = 0,trim_head_lines = 0):# create output sirectory if outdir is None:outdir = os.path.join (os.path.dirname (file),'split') if not os.path.exists (outdir):os.mkdir (outdir) # read input file with open (file,'r') as f:lines = f.readlines () # get file extension extension = os.path.splitext (file) [ - 1 ] # grab global header rows global_header = lines [:global_header_rows ] # find indices of lines containing split_pattern starts = [ ] for i,line in enumerate (lines):if re.search (split_pattern,line):starts.append (i) starts.append (len (lines)) # get length of lines # split lines into segments based on positions of regex splits = { } for i in range (len (starts) - 1):m = re.search (fname_pattern,lines [ starts [ i ] ]) if m:fname = m.groups () [ 0 ].strip () else:fname = 'no_name_{:}'.format (i) splits [ fname ] = global_header + lines [ starts [ i ]:starts [ i + 1 ] ] [ trim_head_lines:trim_tail_lines ] # write files print ('Writing files to: {:}'.format (outdir)) for k,v in splits.items ():fname = (k + extension).replace (' ','_') with open (os.path.join (outdir,fname),'w') as f:f.writelines (v) print ('  {:}'.format (fname)) print ('Done.') return outdir

If so, it calculates the Bayesian mean (`bm`), variance (`bv`), and standard deviation (`bs`) of the non-NaN values using the `bayes_mvs` function. If there are more than two non-NaN values in the array, it calculates the median and IQR of these values, then returns a new array where each non-NaN value is transformed using the formula `(value - median) / IQR`. ### Summary:
The `noise_despike` function is designed to remove spikes from a signal (`sig`). It uses a convolution-based approach to identify and replace values that deviate significantly from the local mean. The function iteratively identifies spikes and replaces them with the local mean until no more spikes are detected or a maximum number of iterations (`maxiter`) is reached.

- **Parameters:**
  - `sig`: The input signal array.
  - `win`: The size of the convolution window (default is 3). It must be an odd number.
  - `nlim`: The number of standard deviations above or below the mean to consider a value a spike (default is 24.0).
  - `maxiter`: The maximum number of iterations to perform (default is 4).

- **Process:**
  1. Ensure the convolution window size (`win`) is odd.
  2. Create a convolution kernel and initialize a boolean array (`over`) to track which elements are considered spikes.
  3. Pad the edges of the boolean array to avoid edge effects.
  4. Iterate up to `maxiter` times:
     - Compute the local mean (`rmean`) and standard deviation (`rstd`) using convolution.
     - Identify elements that are spikes based on the condition `sig > rmean + nlim * rstd` or `sig < rmean - nlim * rstd`.
     - Replace identified spikes with the local mean.
  5. Return the despiked signal.
codeFunctions: def noise_despike (sig,win = 3,nlim = 24.,maxiter = 4):if win % 2 != 1:win += 1 # win must be odd kernel = np.ones (win) / win # make convolution kernel over = np.ones (len (sig),dtype = bool) # initialize bool array # pad edges to avoid edge-effects npad = int ((win - 1) / 2) over [:npad ] = False over [ - npad:] = False # set up monitoring nloops = 0 # do the despiking while any (over) and (nloops < maxiter):rmean = np.convolve (sig,kernel,'valid') # mean by convolution rstd = rmean ** 0.5 # std = sqrt(signal), because count statistics # identify where signal > mean + std * nlim (OR signa < mean - std * # nlim) # | (sig[npad:-npad] < rmean - nlim * rstd) over [ npad:- npad ] = (sig [ npad:- npad ] > rmean + nlim * rstd) # if any are over, replace them with mean of neighbours if any (over):# replace with values either side # sig[over] = sig[np.roll(over, -1) | np.roll(over, 1)].reshape((sum(over), 2)).mean(1) # replace with mean sig [ npad:- npad ] [ over [ npad:- npad ] ] = rmean [ over [ npad:- npad ] ] nloops += 1 # repeat until no more removed. return sig

codeComment:
### Summary:
The `expdecay_despike` function is designed to remove spikes from a signal (`sig`) that are not consistent with an expected exponential decay pattern. The function calculates the root mean square (RMS) noise level of the signal, initially based on the first 5 points and then expanding up to 50 points if the noise level does not increase dramatically. It then iteratively identifies and replaces points in the signal that fall outside the expected range defined by an exponential decay model, considering the RMS noise. The process is repeated up to a maximum number of iterations (`maxiter`), defaulting to 3, until no more spikes are detected. The function returns the despiked signal.
codeFunctions: def expdecay_despike (sig,expdecay_coef,tstep,maxiter = 3):# determine rms noise of data noise = np.std (sig [:5 ]) # initially, calculated based on first 5 points # expand the selection up to 50 points, unless it dramatically increases  # the std (i.e. catches the 'laser on' region) for i in [ 10,20,30,50 ]:inoise = np.std (sig [:i ]) if inoise < 1.5 * noise:noise = inoise rms_noise3 = 3 * noise i = 0 f = True while (i < maxiter) and f:# calculate low and high possibles values based on exponential decay siglo = np.roll (sig * np.exp (tstep * expdecay_coef),1) sighi = np.roll (sig * np.exp (- tstep * expdecay_coef),- 1) # identify points that are outside these limits, beyond what might be explained # by noise in the data loind = (sig < siglo - rms_noise3) & (sig < np.roll (sig,- 1) - rms_noise3) hiind = (sig > sighi + rms_noise3) & (sig > np.roll (sig,1) + rms_noise3) # replace all such values with their preceding sig [ loind ] = sig [ np.roll (loind,- 1) ] sig [ hiind ] = sig [ np.roll (hiind,- 1) ] f = any (np.concatenate ([ loind,hiind ])) i += 1 return sig

1. **Reading the Log File:**

2. **Identifying Hash Lines:**

3. **Extracting Paths:**
   - Using a regular expression, it extracts key-value pairs of paths from the lines between the first and last hash lines.
   - These paths are then joined with the directory name of the log file to form absolute paths, stored in the `paths` dictionary.

4. **Extracting Function Calls:**
   - Another regular expression is used to parse function calls and their arguments and keyword arguments from lines after the second hash line.
   - Each function call is stored as a tuple containing the function name and a dictionary of arguments and keyword arguments, appended to the `runargs` list.

5. **Modifying `__init__` Calls:**
   - If a function call is `__init__`, it modifies the keyword arguments to set specific values for `config`, `dataformat`, and `data_folder`.

6. **Returning Results:**

The method `estimate_tx_gas_with_web3` estimates the gas required for a transaction on the Ethereum network using the Web3 library. It takes the following parameters:
- `safe_address`: The address of the sender (safe).
- `to`: The recipient address of the transaction.
- `value`: The amount of Ether to be sent in the transaction.

The method returns an integer representing the estimated gas cost for the transaction, using the `estimate_gas` function of the `ethereum_client` with the block identifier set to 'pending'.

originalComment: Estimate tx gas.Use the max of calculation using safe method and web3 if operation == CALL or use just the safe calculation otherwise
codeComment:
### Summary:
The `estimate_tx_gas` method calculates the estimated gas cost for a transaction involving a Safe contract. It considers the gas costs for routing through a proxy and nested calls. The method first sets a base gas cost for these operations. It then estimates the gas cost using the Safe contract's estimation method and adds the base costs. If the operation is a CALL, it also attempts to estimate the gas cost using Web3 and adds the base costs. The method returns the maximum of the two gas estimations (Safe and Web3) if the operation is a CALL; otherwise, it returns the Safe gas estimation. If the Web3 estimation fails, it defaults to zero.
codeFunctions: def estimate_tx_gas (self,safe_address:str,to:str,value:int,data:bytes,operation:int) -> int:# Costs to route through the proxy and nested calls proxy_gas = 1000 # https://github.com/ethereum/solidity/blob/dfe3193c7382c80f1814247a162663a97c3f5e67/libsolidity/codegen/ExpressionCompiler.cpp#L1764 # This was `false` before solc 0.4.21 -> `m_context.evmVersion().canOverchargeGasForCall()` # So gas needed by caller will be around 35k old_call_gas = 35000 safe_gas_estimation = (self.estimate_tx_gas_with_safe (safe_address,to,value,data,operation) + proxy_gas + old_call_gas) # We cannot estimate DELEGATECALL (different storage) if SafeOperation (operation) == SafeOperation.CALL:try:web3_gas_estimation = (self.estimate_tx_gas_with_web3 (safe_address,to,value,data) + proxy_gas + old_call_gas) except ValueError:web3_gas_estimation = 0 return max (safe_gas_estimation,web3_gas_estimation) else:return safe_gas_estimation

### Summary:
The `_exit` method is designed to handle the exit of a context manager. It takes four parameters: `self`, `obj`, `type`, `value`, and `traceback`. The method checks if an exception occurred during the context execution by examining the `type` parameter.

- If no exception occurred (`type is None`), it attempts to advance the generator `obj` using `obj.next()`. If `obj` raises a `StopIteration` exception, it indicates that the resource was closed as expected, and the method returns. If `obj` yields more than once, a `RuntimeError` is raised.

- If an exception occurred (`type is not None`), the method attempts to pass the exception to the generator `obj` using `obj.throw(type, value, traceback)`. If `obj` raises a `StopIteration` exception, it checks if the exception is the same as the one passed to `throw()`. If they are the same, it suppresses the exception; otherwise, it re-raises it. If `obj` does not raise a `StopIteration` exception, a `RuntimeError` is raised indicating that the resource did not close after `throw()`.

- If any other exception occurs during the handling of the exception, it checks if the current exception is the same as the one passed to `throw()`. If they are different, it re-raises the current exception. This ensures that the `_exit` method does not raise an exception unless it itself fails.
codeFunctions: def _exit (self,obj,type,value,traceback):if type is None:# No in-context exception occurred try:obj.next () except StopIteration:# Resource closed as expected return else:raise RuntimeError ('{} yielded more than once.'.format (obj)) else:# In-context exception occurred try:obj.throw (type,value,traceback) raise RuntimeError ('{} did not close after throw()'.format (obj)) except StopIteration as exc:# Suppress the exception *unless* it's the same exception that # was passed to throw().  This prevents a StopIteration # raised inside the "with" statement from being suppressed return exc is not value except:# only re-raise if it's *not* the exception that was # passed to throw(), because __exit__() must not raise # an exception unless __exit__() itself failed.  But # resource.throw() will raise the exception to signal propagation, # so this fixes the impedance mismatch between the throw() protocol # and the __exit__() protocol. # # Middleware or Resources that throw exceptions before yielding # will just rethrow the same exception here which is expected. They # won't have a chance to do anything about the exception though which # seems OK since they never got to the point of being ready anyway. if sys.exc_info () [ 1 ] is not value:raise

It takes two parameters: `wavelength`, which is the wavelength of light, and `coefficients`, a list of coefficients for the Cauchy equation. The function iterates over the coefficients, calculates the contribution of each coefficient to the refractive index based on the formula \( n += \frac{c}{\text{wavelength}^{2i}} \), where `i` is the index of the coefficient in the list, and sums these contributions to return the final refractive index `n`.

1. **Authentication**: Attempts to authenticate with a backend service using provided credentials (`username` and `password`).
2. **Exception Handling**: Catches and logs any `BackendException` that occurs during authentication, prints an error message, and exits the program with an error code if authentication fails.

codeComment:
### Summary:
The `login` method is designed to handle user authentication with optional token generation. It accepts a username, password, an optional `generate` parameter (default is 'enabled'), and an optional `proxies` dictionary. The method performs the following steps:

1. Logs a debug message with the username and generate parameter.
2. Checks if the username and password are provided; raises a `BackendException` if either is missing.
3. Validates the proxy protocols if proxies are provided; raises a `BackendException` for invalid protocols.
4. Sets the proxies if provided.
5. Constructs a JSON payload with the username and password.
6. If `generate` is set to 'force', it adds an 'action' key to the JSON payload and logs a debug message.
7. Sends a POST request to the 'login' endpoint with the JSON payload.
8. If the response status code is 401, logs an error and returns `False`.
9. Decodes the response and checks for a 'token' key.
10. If a token is found, sets the token and returns `True`.
11. If `generate` is 'force' and no token is provided, raises a `BackendException`.
12. If `generate` is 'disabled', logs an error and returns `False`.
13. If `generate` is 'enabled' and no token is provided, logs a warning and recursively calls `login` with `generate` set to 'force'.
14. Returns `False` if none of the above conditions are met.
codeFunctions: def login (self,username,password,generate = 'enabled',proxies = None):logger.debug ("login for: %s with generate: %s",username,generate) if not username or not password:raise BackendException (BACKEND_ERROR,"Missing mandatory parameters") if proxies:for key in proxies.keys ():try:assert key in PROXY_PROTOCOLS except AssertionError:raise BackendException (BACKEND_ERROR,"Wrong proxy protocol ",key) self.proxies = proxies endpoint = 'login' json = { u'username':username,u'password':password } if generate == 'force':json [ 'action' ] = 'generate' logger.debug ("Asking for generating new token") response = self.get_response (method = 'POST',endpoint = endpoint,json = json) if response.status_code == 401:logger.error ("Backend refused login with params %s",json) self.set_token (token = None) return False resp = self.decode (response = response) if 'token' in resp:self.set_token (token = resp [ 'token' ]) return True if generate == 'force':# pragma: no cover - need specific backend tests self.set_token (token = None) raise BackendException (BACKEND_ERROR,"Token not provided") if generate == 'disabled':# pragma: no cover - need specific backend tests logger.error ("Token disabled ... to be implemented!") return False if generate == 'enabled':# pragma: no cover - need specific backend tests logger.warning ("Token enabled, but none provided, require new token generation") return self.login (username,password,'force') return False

codeComment:
### Summary:
The `get_all` method is designed to retrieve all items from a specified endpoint by handling pagination. It supports both single-threaded and multi-threaded processing based on the `self.processes` attribute.

- **Parameters:**
  - `endpoint`: The API endpoint from which to retrieve data.
  - `params`: Optional dictionary of parameters for the GET request. If not provided, it defaults to a dictionary with `max_results` set to `BACKEND_PAGINATION_LIMIT`.

- **Process Flow:**
  1. **Single-threaded Processing (`self.processes == 1`):**
     - Continuously fetches data from the endpoint until there are no more pages (`last_page` is `True`).
     - Updates the `params` dictionary to request the next page of results.
     - Collects all items into the `items` list.

  2. **Multi-threaded Processing (`self.processes > 1`):**
     - Determines the total number of pages required based on the initial response's metadata.
     - Divides the pages among multiple processes using a queue (`out_q`) to collect results.
     - Each process fetches a chunk of pages and puts the results into the queue.
     - The main process collects all results from the queue and combines them into a single list of items.

- **Return Value:**
  - A dictionary containing all retrieved items under the key `_items` and a status message `_status` set to `'OK'`.

### Helper Function:
- **`get_pages`:**
  - A helper function used by the multi-threaded process to fetch a range of pages and put the results into a queue.
  - **Parameters:**
    - `endpoint`: The API endpoint.
    - `params`: Parameters for the GET request.
    - `pages`: A list of page numbers to fetch.
    - `out_q`: A multiprocessing queue to store the fetched items.
codeFunctions:
def get_all (self,endpoint,params = None):# pylint: disable=too-many-locals # Set max results at maximum value supported by the backend to limit requests number if not params:params = { 'max_results':BACKEND_PAGINATION_LIMIT } elif params and 'max_results' not in params:params [ 'max_results' ] = BACKEND_PAGINATION_LIMIT # Get first page last_page = False items = [ ] if self.processes == 1:while not last_page:# Get elements ... resp = self.get (endpoint = endpoint,params = params) # Response contains: # _items: # ... # _links: #  self, parent, prev, last, next # _meta: # - max_results, total, page if 'next' in resp [ '_links' ]:# Go to next page ... params [ 'page' ] = int (resp [ '_meta' ] [ 'page' ]) + 1 params [ 'max_results' ] = int (resp [ '_meta' ] [ 'max_results' ]) else:last_page = True items.extend (resp [ '_items' ]) else:def get_pages (endpoint,params,pages,out_q):"""
                Function to get pages loaded by multiprocesses

                :param endpoint: endpoint to get data
                :type endpoint: string
                :param params: parameters for get request
                :type params: dict
                :param pages: range of pages to get
                :type pages: list
                :param out_q: Queue object
                :type out_q: multiprocessing.Queue
                :return: None
                """ multi_items = [ ] for page in pages:params [ 'page' ] = page resp = self.get (endpoint,params) multi_items.extend (resp [ '_items' ]) out_q.put (multi_items) # Get first page resp = self.get (endpoint,params) number_pages = int (math.ceil (float (resp [ '_meta' ] [ 'total' ]) / float (resp [ '_meta' ] [ 'max_results' ]))) out_q = multiprocessing.Queue () chunksize = int (math.ceil (number_pages / float (self.processes))) procs = [ ] for i in range (self.processes):begin = i * chunksize end = begin + chunksize if end > number_pages:end = number_pages begin += 1 end += 1 p = multiprocessing.Process (target = get_pages,args = (endpoint,params,range (begin,end),out_q)) procs.append (p) p.start () # Collect all results into a single result dict. We know how many dicts # with results to expect. for i in range (self.processes):items.extend (out_q.get ()) # Wait for all worker processes to finish for p in procs:p.join () return { '_items':items,'_status':'OK' }

### Summary:
The `patch` method sends a PATCH request to a specified endpoint with provided data and headers. It requires the `If-Match` header for the request. If the response status code is 200, it decodes and returns the response. If the status code is 412 (Precondition Failed), it checks if the `inception` flag is set. If true, it updates the `If-Match` header with the current etag from a GET request to the same endpoint and retries the PATCH request. If the status code is neither 200 nor 412, it raises a `BackendException` with the status code and response content.
codeFunctions: def patch (self,endpoint,data,headers = None,inception = False):if not headers:raise BackendException (BACKEND_ERROR,"Header If-Match required for patching an object") response = self.get_response (method = 'PATCH',endpoint = endpoint,json = data,headers = headers) if response.status_code == 200:return self.decode (response = response) if response.status_code == 412:# 412 means Precondition failed, but confirm ... if inception:# update etag and retry to patch resp = self.get (endpoint) headers = { 'If-Match':resp [ '_etag' ] } return self.patch (endpoint,data = data,headers = headers,inception = False) raise BackendException (response.status_code,response.content) else:# pragma: no cover - should never occur raise BackendException (response.status_code,response.content)

The `create` function is designed to create a junction point (a type of directory symbolic link) on a Windows file system. It takes two parameters: `source`, which is the path to the directory that the junction point will point to, and `link_name`, which is the name of the junction point to be created.

1. **Validation**:
   - The function first checks if the `source` is a valid directory. If not, it raises an exception.

3. **Directory Creation**:

4. **Reparse Point Creation**:
   - The function acquires a handle to the newly created directory with specific flags to allow reparse point operations.
   - It constructs a reparse point buffer containing the target path (`source`).
   - Using the `DeviceIoControl` function, it sets the reparse point data for the directory, effectively creating the junction point.

5. **Error Handling**:
   - If any step fails (e.g., invalid handle, `DeviceIoControl` failure), the function raises a `WinError`.
   - If the junction point creation is successful, the `success` flag is set to `True`.

6. **Cleanup**:
   - The handle to the directory is closed in the `finally` block to ensure resources are released.
   - If the junction point creation fails, the newly created directory is removed to clean up.

This function is specific to Windows and relies on Windows API functions for creating junction points.

The `_init_population_stats` method calculates the mean and standard deviation of a specific tag value across all samples in a VCF file. It initializes counters and accumulators, iterates through each VCF record, extracts the relevant tag value, and updates the mean and variance using Welford's online algorithm. The method handles file opening and closing, and returns the computed mean and standard deviation rounded to a specified precision. If no valid values are found, it returns `None` for both mean and standard deviation.
codeFunctions: def _init_population_stats (self,vcf_reader,dependent_tag_id):#pylint: disable=invalid-name n = 0 mean = 0 M2 = 0 try:vcf_reader.open () for vcf_record in vcf_reader.vcf_records ():for tag_values in vcf_record.sample_tag_values.values ():value = self._get_dependent_value (tag_values,dependent_tag_id) if value is not None:n += 1 delta = value - mean mean += delta / n M2 += delta * (value - mean) finally:vcf_reader.close () mean = round (mean,self._MAX_PRECISION) stdev = 0 if n == 0:mean = None stdev = None elif n >= 2:variance = M2 / n stdev = round (math.sqrt (variance),self._MAX_PRECISION) return mean,stdev

1. **Initial Setup**: The method starts by storing the current file pointer position in `where` and initializing `offset` to 0.

2. **Reading Data**: It enters a loop where it reads a chunk of data from the file using `self.read(self.read_size)`, storing the length of the data in `data_len` and the data itself in `data`.

3. **Handling End of File**: If `data_len` is 0, indicating the end of the file, the loop breaks.

4. **Special Handling for `\r\n`**: If the line terminator `\r\n` is in `self.LINE_TERMINATORS` and the last byte of the read data is `\r`, it reads one more byte to check if it is `\n`. If it is, it appends `\n` to `data` and adjusts `data_len`.

5. **Seeking Line Terminator**: The method then iterates through `data` to find a line terminator using `self.prefix_line_terminator(data[data_where:])`. If a terminator is found, it seeks the file pointer to the position right after the terminator and returns the new file pointer position.

6. **Adjusting Offsets**: If no terminator is found in the current chunk, it increments `data_where` and `offset` and continues reading the next chunk of data.

7. **Return Value**: If no line terminator is found after reading through the file, the method returns -1, indicating the end of the file or no more lines.

### Summary:
The `seek_previous_line` method is designed to move the file pointer to the beginning of the previous line in a file. It starts by storing the current file pointer position (`where`) and initializing an `offset` to zero. The method then enters a loop where it reads chunks of data from the file, moving backwards from the current position, to find the start of the previous line.

If the file uses the `\r\n` line terminator and the first byte of the read data is a newline (`\n`), it checks if the preceding byte is a carriage return (`\r`). If so, it adjusts the data to include the `\r` and updates the file pointer accordingly.

The method looks for a line terminator in the read data. If a terminator is found and it is at the end of the data, it is ignored as it belongs to the current line. If a terminator is found elsewhere, the file pointer is moved to the start of the previous line, and the method returns the new file pointer position.

If no line terminator is found, the method continues to read backwards until it either finds a terminator or reaches the beginning of the file. If the file pointer is already at the beginning of the file, it returns `-1`. If it reaches the very first line, it sets the file pointer to the start of the file and returns `0`.

def seek_previous_line (self):where = self.file.tell () offset = 0 while True:if offset == where:break read_size = self.read_size if self.read_size <= where else where self.file.seek (where - offset - read_size,SEEK_SET) data_len,data = self.read (read_size) # Consider the following example: Foo | 
Bar where " | " denotes current position, # '
Bar' is the read part and 'Foo' is the remaining part. # We should completely consume terminator "
" by reading one extra byte. if b'
' in self.LINE_TERMINATORS and data [ 0 ] == b'

codeComment:
### Summary:
The `tail` method reads the last `lines` number of lines from a file. It starts by seeking to the end of the file and then iteratively moves backward to find the start of each line. If it encounters fewer lines than requested, it breaks out of the loop. After reading the data, it removes any trailing line terminators that are not between lines. Finally, it returns the lines as a list of strings, or an empty list if no data is found.
codeFunctions: def tail (self,lines = 10):self.file.seek (0,SEEK_END) for i in range (lines):if self.seek_previous_line () == - 1:break data = self.file.read () for t in self.LINE_TERMINATORS:if data.endswith (t):# Only terminators _between_ lines should be preserved. # Otherwise terminator of the last line will be treated as separtaing line and empty line. data = data [:- len (t) ] break if data:return self.splitlines (data) else:return [ ]

### Summary:
The `head` method reads the first `lines` number of lines from a file associated with the object. It starts by seeking to the beginning of the file. It then iterates up to `lines` times, attempting to move to the next line each time. If it reaches the end of the file before reading the specified number of lines, it breaks out of the loop. The method then reads the data up to the current position, ensuring that the terminator of the last line is not included unless it is between lines. Finally, it returns the data split into lines or an empty list if no data is read.

originalComment: Iterator generator that returns lines as data is added to the file.
codeComment:
### Summary:
The `follow` method is designed to continuously read new lines from a file, similar to the `tail -f` command in Unix. It handles file truncation and ignores line terminators that are added at the end of the file before a new line starts. The method uses a loop to check the current file position and read new lines as they are appended to the file. If the file is truncated, it resets the position to the beginning. It yields each new line read from the file, or `None` if no new line is available.
codeFunctions: def follow (self):trailing = True while True:where = self.file.tell () if where > os.fstat (self.file.fileno ()).st_size:# File was truncated. where = 0 self.file.seek (where) line = self.file.readline () if line:if trailing and line in self.LINE_TERMINATORS:# This is just the line terminator added to the end of the file # before a new line, ignore. trailing = False continue terminator = self.suffix_line_terminator (line) if terminator:line = line [:- len (terminator) ] trailing = False yield line else:trailing = True self.file.seek (where) yield None

### Summary:

It takes four parameters: `cls` (the class itself, not used in the method), `sample_names` (a list of sample names), `rformat` (a string representing the format of the sample fields), and `sample_fields` (a list of sample fields corresponding to each sample). The method returns an `OrderedDict` where each key is a sample name and each value is another `OrderedDict` mapping tag names to their corresponding values for that sample. The tag names are derived from the `rformat` string, which is split into a list of tag names using the `_format_list` method of the `VcfRecord` class. Each sample field is split by the colon (`:`) character to separate the tag values, which are then zipped with the tag names to form the nested `OrderedDict` structure. codeFunctions: def _sample_tag_values (cls,sample_names,rformat,sample_fields):sample_tag_values = OrderedDict () tag_names = VcfRecord._format_list (rformat) for i,sample_field in enumerate (sample_fields):tag_values = sample_field.split (":") if sample_field else "." sample_tag_values [ sample_names [ i ] ] = OrderedDict (zip (tag_names,tag_values)) return sample_tag_values

datetime.datetime.utcnow ()).total_seconds () else:timeToSleep = 0.0 time.sleep (timeToSleep) # Then try to fetch the next state file sqnStr = str (int (state [ 'sequenceNumber' ]) + 1).zfill (9) url = '%s/%s/%s/%s.state.txt' % (base_url,sqnStr [ 0:3 ],sqnStr [ 3:6 ],sqnStr [ 6:9 ]) delay = 1.0 while True:try:u = urllib2.urlopen (url) interval_fudge -= (interval_fudge / 2.0) break except urllib2.HTTPError as e:if e.code == 404:time.sleep (delay) delay = min (delay * 2,13) interval_fudge += delay if state_dir:with open ('%s/state.txt' % state_dir,'w') as f:f.write (u.read ()) with open ('%s/state.txt' % state_dir,'r') as f:state = readState (f) else:state = readState (u)

### Summary:
The `iter_osm_notes` function is designed to continuously fetch and parse notes from the OpenStreetMap (OSM) API. It retrieves notes in an RSS feed format, processes them to identify actions such as note creation, commenting, and closing, and yields these notes in chronological order. The function accepts parameters to limit the number of notes fetched per request (`feed_limit`), set the interval between requests (`interval`), and determine whether to parse timestamps (`parse_timestamps`). codeFunctions: def iter_osm_notes (feed_limit = 25,interval = 60,parse_timestamps = True):last_seen_guid = None while True:u = urllib2.urlopen ('https://www.openstreetmap.org/api/0.6/notes/feed?limit=%d' % feed_limit) tree = etree.parse (u) new_notes = [ ] for note_item in tree.xpath ('/rss/channel/item'):title = note_item.xpath ('title') [ 0 ].text if title.startswith ('new note ('):action = 'create' elif title.startswith ('new comment ('):action = 'comment' elif title.startswith ('closed note ('):action = 'close' # Note that (at least for now) the link and guid are the same in the feed. guid = note_item.xpath ('link') [ 0 ].text if last_seen_guid == guid:break elif last_seen_guid == None:# The first time through we want the first item to be the "last seen" # because the RSS feed is newest-to-oldest last_seen_guid = guid else:note_id = int (guid.split ('/') [ - 1 ].split ('#c') [ 0 ]) new_notes.append ((action,get_note (note_id,parse_timestamps))) # We yield the reversed list because we want to yield in change order # (i.e. "oldest to most current") for note in reversed (new_notes):yield note yield model.Finished (None,None) time.sleep (interval)
